items.title: Antonelli wins Madrid's debut race as a VSC undoes Norris
items.summary: Kimi Antonelli took his eighth win of the season, beating Max Verstappen and pole-sitter Lando Norris. Norris led from pole but a Virtual Safety Car for Lance Stroll's stopped Aston Martin fell just after his pit window closed, letting Antonelli and Verstappen pit almost for free and jump him. Lewis Hamilton retired early with a brake issue after contact with Verstappen at the start.
items.why_it_matters: This is the confirmed final result, not a pre-race prediction: Norris finished third, not first, and Hamilton did not finish. Any commentary using the earlier pre-race form guide must be updated to this classification.

items.title: Norris's lost win reopens F1's Virtual Safety Car timing debate
items.summary: The VSC that cost Norris the lead was triggered five seconds after he passed the pit entry and ended just before he could complete his own stop, forcing him to pay the full pit-lane time loss. Sources say the Sporting Advisory Committee will discuss the VSC rules at its next meeting because of this incident.
items.why_it_matters: This is a live rules-review story, not a settled outcome. Do not present the race classification as evidence the VSC rule will change before any committee decision is confirmed.

items.title: Red Bull ordered Verstappen to give back places after a first-lap tangle
items.summary: Verstappen kept third place at the start only after cutting Turn 1 during contact with Hamilton, and Red Bull's Laurent Mekies had him hand the places back to Antonelli and Hamilton to avoid a penalty. Verstappen recovered to finish P2 after Hamilton's retirement and a favourable VSC pit stop.
items.why_it_matters: This explains Verstappen's second place without needing a stewards' penalty — a team-management decision, not a ruling. Keep the causal chain (contact, corner-cut, team instruction, recovery) explicit rather than compressing it into a bare result line.

items.title: Hamilton denies asking for Ferrari staff changes after a difficult post-Spain patch
items.summary: Following an Italian media report (Corriere della Sera) that Hamilton had asked Ferrari to replace trackside personnel and that his relationship with team principal Fred Vasseur had weakened, Hamilton publicly denied the claim on Instagram, saying he has “never asked for anyone on my team to be replaced.” The denial follows Ferrari's podium-less run since Spa in July, an exasperated Hamilton pleading for the team to fix operational errors at Monza, and his retirement from the Madrid race with a brake issue after contact with Verstappen.
items.why_it_matters: This is Hamilton's own on-the-record rebuttal of a specific personnel-change claim, not a confirmed team decision — keep the denial and the underlying rumour clearly separated on air, and do not present the Corriere della Sera report as settled fact.

sources.label: The Race: Hamilton denies Ferrari staff-change claim

items.title: Antonelli extends title lead to 81 points; Russell concedes the fight
items.summary: The Madrid win stretches Antonelli's Drivers' Championship lead over team-mate Russell to 81 points, and Russell has since said he no longer considers himself in the title fight. Use the current standings table for the exact points and gap, since totals change every round.
items.why_it_matters: Supersedes the pre-race framing that the Mercedes contest was still open; the standings and Russell's own words now describe an effectively decided intra-team battle.
